l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson receive a cipher message from Fred Porlock warning that danger threatens a wealthy man named Douglas at Birlstone. Holmes identifies it as a book cipher and decodes it using an older edition of Whitaker’s Almanac, obtaining a warning about Douglas at Birlstone Manor House. Fred Porlock’s accompanying letter says that Professor Moriarty suspects him and asks Holmes to burn the cipher. Inspector Alec MacDonald then arrives and reveals that Mr. Douglas of Birlstone Manor House was horribly murdered the previous night.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Sherlock Holmes examines a cipher message from Fred Porlock and reasons that it refers to numbered words in a large, standardized book printed in double columns. He correctly identifies an older edition of Whitaker’s Almanac as the key and decodes a warning about danger threatening Douglas at Birlstone.

l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Dr. Watson receives and discusses Fred Porlock’s cipher message with Sherlock Holmes. He helps reason through possible source books, identifies the Bible, Bradshaw, and an almanac as possibilities, and records the decoded warning.

l: Fred Porlock, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Fred Porlock sends Sherlock Holmes a cipher message warning of danger to Douglas at Birlstone. In a letter, he says that Professor Moriarty suspects him, refuses to provide the cipher key, and asks Holmes to burn the message.

l: Professor Moriarty, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Professor Moriarty is described by Sherlock Holmes as the controlling criminal brain behind an extensive underworld organization. Fred Porlock fears that Moriarty suspects him of betraying the organization.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Alec MacDonald, an Inspector of Scotland Yard, visits Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson. He recognizes the names Douglas and Birlstone on their decoded message and reports that Mr. Douglas of Birlstone Manor House was murdered the previous night.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Mr. Douglas is identified in the decoded warning as a rich country gentleman residing at Birlstone. Alec MacDonald reports that he was horribly murdered the previous night.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Birlstone Manor House is identified as the residence of Mr. Douglas in the decoded warning. It is associated with the reported murder of Mr. Douglas.

l: the cipher message, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The cipher message consists of numbered references, including the words Douglas and Birlstone. Sherlock Holmes decodes it as a warning that danger may come very soon to a rich man named Douglas at Birlstone.

l: the anonymous warning letter, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The coded warning concerns imminent danger to Douglas, a rich country gentleman at Birlstone. Its meaning is recovered by using numbered words from an older edition of Whitaker’s Almanac.

l: Whitaker’s Almanac, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: Sherlock Holmes tests the cipher against the current edition of Whitaker’s Almanac but obtains meaningless words. He then uses an older edition and finds that its numbered words produce the warning about danger to Douglas at Birlstone.

l: the book cipher, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The book cipher uses a page, a column, and numbered words to convey a secret message. Sherlock Holmes concludes that the book must be common, standardized, large, and printed in double columns, ultimately identifying Whitaker’s Almanac.

l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The Douglas murder is revealed by Alec MacDonald after Sherlock Holmes decodes the warning concerning Douglas at Birlstone. Mr. Douglas of Birlstone Manor House was horribly murdered the previous night.

l: the warning, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The warning states that danger may come very soon to Douglas, a rich country gentleman at Birlstone. Its significance is confirmed when Alec MacDonald reports Douglas’s murder.

l: the letter from Fred Porlock, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The letter from Fred Porlock says that Professor Moriarty suspects Porlock and that Porlock will go no further in the matter. It asks Sherlock Holmes to burn the cipher message, which Porlock believes can no longer be useful.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, PART I / Chapter I
s: The murder of Mr. Douglas is reported by Inspector Alec MacDonald at the end of the unit. Mr. Douglas, of Birlstone Manor House, was horribly murdered the previous night.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Sherlock Holmes explains to Inspector MacDonald that the anonymous warning from Porlock foretold the death of John Douglas at Birlstone and may connect the murder to Professor Moriarty. Holmes argues that Moriarty secretly controls a large criminal organization, with Colonel Sebastian Moran as his chief of staff, and suggests that Moriarty’s wealth is acquired illegally. MacDonald and Holmes travel to Birlstone after receiving White Mason’s report describing a perplexing murder involving a shotgun wound to Douglas’s head. Holmes avoids forming a premature theory and intends to trace the connection between Moriarty in London and the dead man in Sussex.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Sherlock Holmes is interested rather than surprised when he learns that John Douglas has been murdered, because Porlock’s anonymous warning had predicted danger to a certain person. He explains his suspicions about Professor Moriarty’s criminal organization, wealth, and possible connection to the murder, then travels with Inspector MacDonald to Birlstone to investigate.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Inspector MacDonald discusses the warning letter and the Birlstone case with Sherlock Holmes. He initially favors finding Porlock in London but agrees to travel to Birlstone, where he expects to receive fuller details from White Mason.

l: Professor Moriarty, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Professor Moriarty is presented as a highly learned and talented man whose unexplained wealth includes ownership of a valuable Greuze painting. Sherlock Holmes believes Moriarty is the hidden force behind London criminals, pays Colonel Sebastian Moran six thousand pounds a year, maintains numerous bank accounts, and rules his organization with a death penalty for disobedience.

l: Fred Porlock, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Porlock is the assumed name of the person who sent Sherlock Holmes an anonymous warning that danger threatened a particular person. Porlock’s warning was followed within an hour by the murder of John Douglas, but Holmes has not attempted to trace Porlock because he promised to keep faith.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: John Douglas is the man whose approaching fate was known through Porlock’s warning. He has been murdered at Birlstone, suffering fatal head injuries from a shotgun discharge.

l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: White Mason is the local officer at Birlstone and a personal friend of Inspector MacDonald. He sends MacDonald a private message describing the case as exceptionally perplexing and asks that Sherlock Holmes be brought to investigate.

l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: Birlstone is the Sussex location where John Douglas has been murdered. Sherlock Holmes, Inspector MacDonald, and the narrator travel there to investigate the case’s extraordinary features.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: The Birlstone murder concerns the killing of John Douglas shortly before midnight. The available report states that it is undoubtedly murder, involves a shotgun wound to the head, has produced no arrest, and presents perplexing and extraordinary features.

l: the anonymous warning letter, The Valley of Fear, Chapter II
s: The anonymous warning letter was sent to Sherlock Holmes from Camberwell and warned that danger threatened a certain person. It was associated with a cipher and was followed by the actual death of John Douglas; the letter was sent by someone using the name Porlock.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The unit introduces Birlstone, its ancient Manor House, and the household of John Douglas and Mrs. Douglas. Cecil James Barker discovers that Douglas has been murdered in the Manor House by a close-range blast from a sawed-off shotgun, while the raised drawbridge appears to make escape impossible. Sergeant Wilson, Dr. Wood, and Ames examine the scene and find evidence that someone hid in the room, escaped through the open window across the moat, left a card marked “V.V. 341,” and removed Douglas’s wedding ring. The unexplained brand on Douglas’s forearm and the other unusual evidence deepen the mystery.

l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The tragedy concerns the murder of John Douglas at the Manor House in Birlstone and the puzzling evidence surrounding the crime. The events bring Cecil James Barker, Sergeant Wilson, Dr. Wood, Ames, and the household servants into the investigation.

l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Birlstone is a small, ancient village on the northern border of Sussex, about ten or twelve miles west of Tunbridge Wells. Its picturesque setting and growing population have attracted well-to-do residents and led to the development of shops.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Birlstone Manor House is an ancient, many-gabled building surrounded by an inner moat and approached only by a drawbridge. John Douglas and Mrs. Douglas took possession of it after it had stood untenanted and begun to decay, and John Douglas was murdered there on the night of January 6th.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: John Douglas was about fifty, vigorous, genial, generous, and reputed to have made his money in the California gold fields. He was found dead on the floor of the Manor House in a pink dressing gown after receiving a shotgun blast in the face, and he bore a distinctive brand on his right forearm.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Mrs. Douglas was a tall, dark, slender Englishwoman about twenty years younger than John Douglas. She was retiring and devoted to her household, but had sometimes shown acute uneasiness when her husband was late returning; after the shot, she came downstairs and was taken away by Mrs. Allen before seeing the body.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Cecil James Barker was a wealthy English bachelor and an intimate friend of John Douglas from America. He heard the shot, reached the room within about thirty seconds, reported the murder, and told Sergeant Wilson that the open window and blood mark on the sill indicated that the killer escaped across the moat.

l: Sergeant Wilson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Sergeant Wilson was in charge of the small local police station and arrived at the Manor House shortly after midnight. He questioned Barker and Ames, examined the crime scene, and concluded that the case was too difficult for him alone and would likely require London assistance.

l: Dr. Wood, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Dr. Wood arrived with Sergeant Wilson and Cecil James Barker and immediately recognized that John Douglas was dead. He examined the shattered head and later drew attention to the unusual brand on Douglas’s forearm.

l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: Ames was the prim, respectable, and capable butler of the Manor House. He stated that he had raised the drawbridge at nearly six o’clock, helped enter the room after the murder, identified the missing wedding ring, and confirmed that Douglas had long borne the brand on his forearm.

l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The drawbridge was the only approach to the Manor House and was raised every evening and lowered every morning. It was up from nearly six o’clock until Barker lowered it after the murder, making it appear difficult for an outsider to have entered or escaped.

l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The inner moat was about forty feet wide, surrounded the Manor House, and was fed by a small stream. The open window and a muddy, blood-like mark on its sill led Barker and Sergeant Wilson to believe that the murderer had waded across it.

l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The sawed-off shotgun lay across John Douglas’s chest after being fired at close range. Its barrel had been cut off about a foot in front of the triggers, and the triggers had been wired together so that the whole charge would discharge simultaneously.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: John Douglas’s murder occurred at about half-past eleven in the Manor House. He was found in a room with his head almost destroyed by a shotgun blast, while evidence suggested that a person had hidden behind the curtains, killed him, and escaped through the window.

l: the open window escape, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The long, diamond-paned window was open to its full extent, and a smudge resembling a bloody boot sole marked the wooden sill. Barker and Sergeant Wilson inferred that the murderer left through the window and waded across the moat, although the timing made the escape difficult to explain.

l: card marked V.V. 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: A card bearing the inked inscription “V.V.” and “341” was found beside John Douglas’s body. Sergeant Wilson could not interpret it, and Barker said he had not noticed it before and believed the murderer had left it.

l: the brand on John Douglas's forearm, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: A brown design consisting of a triangle inside a circle was visible halfway up John Douglas’s right forearm. Dr. Wood said it appeared to be a brand rather than a tattoo, while Barker and Ames stated that they had seen it many times before.

l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: John Douglas’s plain gold wedding ring was missing from the little finger of his left hand. Ames explained that it had been worn beneath a nugget ring, which had been removed and then replaced, indicating that someone had deliberately taken the wedding ring.

l: the mystery, The Valley of Fear, Chapter III
s: The mystery involves how a murderer entered the Manor House despite the raised drawbridge, killed John Douglas, and escaped through the open window. The hidden figure, the V.V. 341 card, the branded forearm, and the missing wedding ring leave the circumstances unexplained.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: White Mason meets Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector MacDonald at Birlstone and briefs them on the murder of Mr. Douglas. The investigators examine the Manor House, its moat, the window, the weapons, the footprints, the blood mark, the missing wedding ring, and the card marked V.V. 341. White Mason and MacDonald debate whether the killer came from inside or outside, while Holmes develops questions about a possible secret society and other unexplained clues. Cecil Barker then reports that the suspected killer’s bicycle has been found concealed near the Manor House.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Holmes travels with Dr. Watson to Birlstone and listens closely to White Mason’s account of the case. He examines the shotgun, moat, window, body, blood mark, card, ink, footprints, and dumb-bell, and suggests that the branded mark and card may point to a secret society. He finds White Mason’s outside-killer theory interesting but unconvincing and continues seeking further facts.

l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Holmes to Birlstone and the Manor House. White Mason notes that medical experts, including Dr. Watson, may have a role in interpreting the case.

l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: White Mason, the chief Sussex detective, briefs Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector MacDonald on the murder and leads them through the Manor House. He examines the hammer and shotgun, favors the theory that an outsider entered the house, and suggests that the card and branded mark may indicate a secret society.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Inspector MacDonald challenges the idea that an outsider entered the house, arguing that a deliberate killer would not choose a noisy shotgun when escape was difficult. He agrees that suicide is impossible and accepts that the evidence creates serious difficulties for both an inside and an outside killer.

l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Ames, the butler, is described as white and quivering from shock and is questioned about the house and Mr. Douglas. He confirms that Mr. Douglas often had the branded triangle mark, identifies the plaster on his jaw as a shaving cut, recalls that he seemed restless and excited, and says he has never seen the shotgun in the house.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Cecil Barker is present at the Manor House and is described as tall, sunburned, capable-looking, and masterful. He reports that the suspected killer’s bicycle has been found concealed within a hundred yards of the hall door.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Mr. Douglas has been murdered in the Manor House by a shot from a sawed-off shotgun. His wedding ring is missing, a card marked V.V. 341 lies near him, and he bears a branded triangle inside a circle on his forearm.

l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Birlstone is the Sussex location where the murder occurs and where Holmes, Dr. Watson, White Mason, and Inspector MacDonald meet. The village contains the Manor House and the Westville Arms.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The Manor House is an old Jacobean house surrounded by a moat and approached by a drawbridge. Mr. Douglas is found murdered there, with clues including an open window, mud-stained footprints, a blood mark, a hammer, a shotgun, a card, and a missing wedding ring.

l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Holmes, White Mason, and Inspector MacDonald adopt the existence of a secret society as a working hypothesis based on the card marked V.V. 341 and the branded mark on Mr. Douglas’s forearm. They consider whether an agent of such a society entered the Manor House to carry out vengeance.

l: the police, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The police investigate the murder, examine the weapons and surrounding area, and search for a wet stranger who might have crossed the moat. By the time Holmes arrives, they have found no suspect but have located a bicycle near the Manor House.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The murder of Mr. Douglas is treated as a homicide rather than suicide. The circumstances include a close-range shotgun blast, a missing wedding ring, an open window, a blood mark, footprints, and a card marked V.V. 341, but the killer’s identity and escape remain unexplained.

l: suicide of Mr. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: White Mason and Inspector MacDonald reject the possibility of suicide. They conclude that suicide cannot account for the concealed wedding ring, the staged footprints, the opened window, the blood on the sill, and the other signs.

l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The investigation considers whether the killer was an insider or an outsider and examines the physical clues at the Manor House. Holmes insists on gathering complete evidence before presenting a final theory.

l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The Manor House is surrounded by a broad moat that is about two feet deep at the sides and three feet in the middle. Holmes and White Mason find no clear signs on the far side that anyone climbed out, but agree that a person could cross it without drowning.

l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The drawbridge provides access to the Manor House and had been raised after dusk. White Mason reasons that an outsider could have entered between roughly four-thirty and six, before the bridge was raised.

l: window (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The window immediately to the right of the drawbridge is open as it was found after the murder. It is narrow but large enough for a person to squeeze through, and investigators consider it the suspected killer’s route of escape.

l: the hammer, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The hammer found on the mat is examined and shows no signs of violence or blood. White Mason suggests that Mr. Douglas may have gripped it during a struggle, but the evidence does not establish how it was used.

l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The shotgun is loaded with buckshot cartridges and has its triggers wired together so that pulling the rear trigger fires both barrels. It is less than two feet long, bears the partial name P-E-N, and is identified by Holmes as an American shotgun made by the Pennsylvania Small Arms Company.

l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Mr. Douglas’s wedding ring is missing from his finger. White Mason’s reconstruction supposes that the killer demanded the ring before shooting him, but the reason for its removal remains unknown.

l: card marked V.V. 341, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The rough cardboard card marked V.V. 341 is found beside the dead man. Holmes determines that it was not printed in the room and suggests that, along with the branded mark, it may be connected with a secret society.

l: the brand on John Douglas's forearm, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Mr. Douglas has a branded triangle inside a circle on his forearm, a mark Ames has often seen. Holmes identifies it as a burn that must have caused considerable pain and considers it potentially connected with the card marked V.V. 341.

l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: One dumb-bell is found under the side table in the room. Holmes asks where the other is, but Ames does not know whether there had ever been a pair.

l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: A well-used Rudge-Whitworth bicycle, splashed as if from a considerable journey, is found concealed in evergreens near the Manor House. It has a saddlebag containing a spanner and oilcan but provides no clue to its owner.

l: footprints (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: Indistinct footprints appear in the mud-stained corner behind the curtain and are treated as evidence that someone waited there. The tread on the window sill appears remarkably broad and splay-footed, while the traceable sole in the corner seems more shapely.

l: blood mark (Manor House window sill), The Valley of Fear, Chapter IV
s: The blood mark on the window sill is examined by Holmes with a lens. He identifies it as the tread of a shoe, though its broad shape does not clearly correspond with the other indistinct footprints.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Ames, Mrs. Allen, and Cecil Barker give evidence about the events surrounding the murder of Jack Douglas at Birlstone. Barker says Douglas feared an implacable secret society connected with his past in California, where threatening men sought him after he left. Inspector MacDonald questions Barker about Douglas's marriage, his friendship with Mrs. Douglas, the missing wedding ring, and the alleged connection between the marriage and the tragedy. Sherlock Holmes also questions Barker about the candle and lamp in the study, finding the change in lighting remarkable.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Sherlock Holmes questions Cecil Barker about the candle and lamp in the study. He points out that Barker said the candle was lit when he entered, but that the candle was later out and the lamp was burning.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Inspector MacDonald questions Cecil Barker about Jack Douglas's past in California, the secret society, Douglas's first wife, his marriage to Mrs. Douglas, Barker's friendship with Mrs. Douglas, and the missing wedding ring. He presses Barker when Barker refuses to answer whether Douglas approved of his friendship with his wife.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Jack Douglas was a rich American-made gentleman who had lived at Birlstone for five years. He was described as fearless, kind, and considerate, but he had shown unusual restlessness and irritability on the day before his murder.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Mrs. Douglas came downstairs after the bell rang, but Cecil Barker stopped her and told her that Jack was dead. She returned to her bedroom with Mrs. Allen, where she remained trembling and greatly excited but made no outcry.

l: Ames, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Ames had been Jack Douglas's butler for five years and considered his account of the night clear and sincere. He heard the bell, went to the front of the house with Mrs. Allen, later returned to the study with Barker, and lowered the drawbridge.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Cecil Barker says he believed the murderer escaped through the study window because of the bloodstain and the raised drawbridge. He describes Douglas's unexplained danger, his past in California, his habit of carrying a revolver, his jealousy, and his own loyalty to Douglas and Mrs. Douglas.

l: Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Birlstone is the quiet English place where Jack Douglas rented a house and lived with Mrs. Douglas. Barker believed Douglas's choice of such a secluded place was connected with the danger hanging over him.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The house has a pantry and kitchens at the back, servants' rooms at the extreme rear, and a study at the front. Its drawbridge was raised at night according to the old custom of the house.

l: California, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Jack Douglas lived and worked in California for about five years with Cecil Barker, becoming partners in a successful mining claim at Benito Canyon. Douglas suddenly left for England, and within a week several hard-looking American men came asking where he was.

l: the Eminent Order of Freemen, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Cecil Barker believes that an implacable secret society was pursuing Jack Douglas and would not rest until it killed him. Barker did not know the society's name or the reason Douglas had offended it, but thought the legend on the placard referred to it.

l: the police, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Ames and Barker found the study as the police had seen it after the alarm. Barker went to get the police, who arrived after the servants had been alerted.

l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The murder of Jack Douglas was discovered after the bell rang violently, although Ames and Mrs. Allen had not heard a shot. Barker believed the murderer escaped through the study window, but could not explain what became of the assassin.

l: Douglas's death, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Douglas's death occurred in the study while he was wearing a dressing gown and had left his revolver in the bedroom. Barker said Douglas might have believed he was safe once the drawbridge was raised.

l: Douglas's marriage to Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Douglas's marriage to Mrs. Douglas was questioned because his wedding ring was missing and because Barker acknowledged that Douglas had been jealous of his friendship with his wife. Barker insisted that Mrs. Douglas was loving and faithful.

l: the danger from Mr. Douglas's American past, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The feud against Douglas was believed by Barker to have begun at least eleven years earlier and to have continued with great persistence. Barker thought it had shadowed Douglas's whole life and was connected with the threatening men who sought him in California.

l: the drawbridge, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The drawbridge was raised at night as an old custom of the house. After Douglas was found, Ames lowered it, while Barker argued that its being raised left the study window as the only possible escape route.

l: the bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The bell rang violently after Douglas was killed, bringing Ames, Mrs. Allen, and eventually the others to the front of the house. Its ringing was heard even though the shot itself was not heard by the servants.

l: the study, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The study was where Barker found Douglas and where Ames and Barker later found everything as the police had seen it. The study had a candle on the table when Barker entered, but the candle was later out and the lamp was lit.

l: moat, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The moat was no more than three feet deep at any point. Barker therefore said that the assassin could not possibly have drowned in it.

l: window (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The study window was regarded by Barker as the route by which the murderer escaped. He based this belief on the bloodstain and the fact that the drawbridge was raised.

l: the candle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The candle in the study was lit when Barker entered after the crime. Barker said he blew it out because it gave poor light and then lit the lamp.

l: lamp (Manor House), The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The lamp in the study was burning when Ames and Barker returned to the room. Barker said he lit it to obtain better light after seeing what had happened.

l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Jack Douglas's wedding ring had been removed from his finger. Inspector MacDonald suggested that its absence could connect the marriage with the tragedy, while Barker said it did not reflect upon Mrs. Douglas's honour.

l: the bloodstain, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The bloodstain was considered by Barker to be conclusive evidence that the murderer escaped through the study window.

l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The assassin was believed by Barker to have escaped through the study window. Barker could not explain what became of him or why he had not taken the bicycle believed to be his.

l: Douglas's jealousy, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: Douglas's jealousy concerned his friendship with Cecil Barker and Mrs. Douglas. Barker said Douglas could become angry when he saw sympathy between them, despite loving both his wife and his friend.

l: the alleged affair between Barker and Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter V
s: The alleged affair between Barker and Mrs. Douglas was raised by Inspector MacDonald's questions about whether Douglas approved of their friendship. Barker refused to answer at first, then denied any implication against Mrs. Douglas's honour and declared that she was faithful.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mrs. Douglas tells Inspector MacDonald and Sherlock Holmes that Mr. Douglas feared a danger connected with his American past, though he refused to explain it. She recalls his repeated references to the “Valley of Fear” and his fevered mention of Bodymaster McGinty. The investigators also learn that Mr. Douglas's wedding ring was taken, and Holmes discovers that Cecil Barker's bloodstained carpet slipper matches the blood mark on the study window sill. This suggests that Barker himself made the apparent outside footprint, though Holmes and MacDonald do not yet understand why.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mrs. Douglas tells the investigators that she was stopped by Cecil Barker on the stairs after hearing the shot and never entered the room where the tragedy occurred. She says Mr. Douglas had powerful enemies connected with his American past and repeatedly referred to the Valley of Fear. She also recalls that Bodymaster McGinty was a name he spoke during a fever and that his wedding ring had been taken.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mr. Douglas regularly made a nighttime round of the house because he feared fire. His wife says he believed he was being pursued by powerful enemies from his American life and used the expression “the Valley of Fear” for the danger surrounding him.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Inspector MacDonald questions Mrs. Douglas about the shooting, Mr. Douglas's American past, his marriage, and the missing wedding ring. After Holmes matches Cecil Barker's slipper to the blood mark on the window sill, MacDonald concludes that Barker made the apparent window footprint.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mrs. Douglas about the words associated with Mr. Douglas's past and examines Cecil Barker's carpet slippers. He places one slipper on the blood mark on the study window sill and finds that it exactly corresponds, showing that Barker could have made the mark himself.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Cecil Barker stopped Mrs. Douglas from entering the room after the shooting and went to summon the police. His carpet slippers were stained with blood, and one of them exactly matched the blood mark on the study window sill, indicating that he made the apparent outside footprint.

l: Boss McGinty, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Bodymaster McGinty is a name Mr. Douglas repeatedly spoke with anger and horror while delirious from fever. Mrs. Douglas believes there is a connection between him and the Valley of Fear.

l: America, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: America is identified as the place where Mr. Douglas had lived before his marriage. Mrs. Douglas believes that events there left him in danger from powerful enemies.

l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: The Valley of Fear is Mr. Douglas's expression for a dangerous period or place connected with his American life. He told Mrs. Douglas that he had been in its shadow and feared that they might never escape it.

l: The Tragedy of Birlstone, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: The tragedy occurred in a room that Mrs. Douglas did not enter after hearing the shot. Cecil Barker was present there and later summoned the police.

l: the gunshot, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: The shooting was heard by Mrs. Douglas, who came downstairs after putting on her dressing gown. Cecil Barker stopped her on the stairs a couple of minutes later and told her she could do nothing.

l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mr. Douglas's wedding ring was taken from him. Inspector MacDonald considers its removal extraordinary and questions what motive an enemy could have for taking it.

l: Mr. Barker's carpet slippers, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mr. Barker's carpet slippers were still under the chair in the hall and had bloodstained soles. One slipper exactly matched the blood mark on the study window sill, suggesting that Barker himself made the mark.

l: the danger from Mr. Douglas's American past, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: The danger from Mr. Douglas's American past was something he concealed from Mrs. Douglas to prevent her alarm. She inferred its existence from his precautions, his reactions to unexpected strangers, his references to the Valley of Fear, and his belief that powerful enemies were following him.

l: the enemies from America, The Valley of Fear, Inspector MacDonald had sent up a note to the effect that he would wait
s: Mr. Douglas's enemies were believed by Mrs. Douglas to be powerful and connected with his American life. She says he was always on guard against them and feared that they might eventually reach him.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Dr. Watson encounters Mrs. Douglas and Barker laughing together in the garden, then learns they are anxious about whether Sherlock Holmes would share confidential information with the police. At the village inn, Holmes argues that Barker and Mrs. Douglas are lying about the murder and conspiring to conceal the truth, though he is not certain they committed it. Holmes reasons that the gunshot was probably fired around a quarter to eleven, half an hour before the alarm, and considers the possibility that an outsider murdered Mr. Douglas and threatened the couple into silence. He plans to spend an evening alone in the study and borrows Dr. Watson’s umbrella while the investigation of the bicycle continues.

l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Dr. Watson returns alone to the village inn after the detectives continue their inquiries and walks in the garden. He encounters Mrs. Douglas and Barker together, reports the incident to Sherlock Holmes, and discusses Holmes’s theories about the murder. He lends Holmes his large umbrella.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Sherlock Holmes says he wants no confidential information from Mrs. Douglas or Barker because it could become awkward if they were arrested for conspiracy and murder. He identifies the missing dumb-bell as highly important and argues that Barker’s account is a lie corroborated by Mrs. Douglas. Holmes suspects they are conspiring to conceal the truth, but he remains uncertain whether they committed the murder and plans to spend an evening alone in the study.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Mrs. Douglas is seen laughing with Barker behind a hedge in the garden, apparently having put aside her show of grief. She asks Dr. Watson whether Sherlock Holmes must pass confidential information to the detectives and says that his answer could greatly affect her. Holmes believes that she and Barker are lying and concealing the truth about the murder.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Barker is seen sitting and laughing with Mrs. Douglas in the garden before assuming a solemn manner when Dr. Watson appears. He asks whether Sherlock Holmes acts independently of the police. Holmes says Barker’s account is a clumsy lie and claims that Barker deliberately placed the blood mark on the windowsill to mislead the police.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Mr. Douglas is the dead man whose body was found in the study. Holmes considers the possibility that he had a shameful secret in his past and that an outsider murdered him as an avenger.

l: the village inn, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: The village inn is the modest lodging to which Dr. Watson returns after the detectives continue their inquiries. Sherlock Holmes returns there around five o’clock, eats a substantial tea, and discusses the case with Dr. Watson.

l: the garden, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: The garden beside the village inn contains ancient yew trees, a lawn, and an old sundial. Behind a hedge, Dr. Watson finds Mrs. Douglas and Barker talking and laughing together within hours of Mr. Douglas’s death.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Sherlock Holmes spends the afternoon at the Manor House consulting with his two colleagues. The murder scene and the study are associated with the Manor House.

l: the study, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: The study is where Mr. Douglas’s bloodstained body was found and where the gunshot was apparently fired. Holmes plans to spend an evening alone there, hoping that the room’s atmosphere or further observation will help him solve the case.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Holmes believes the reported sequence surrounding the murder is impossible, particularly the removal and replacement of the wedding ring and the placement of the card. He reasons that the gunshot probably occurred around a quarter to eleven, about half an hour before Barker and Mrs. Douglas raised the alarm.

l: the conspiracy, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Holmes believes Barker and Mrs. Douglas are involved in a conspiracy to conceal the truth about the murder. He also considers an alternative in which they are not the murderers but were threatened by an outsider and then delayed the alarm to protect themselves from suspicion.

l: the gunshot, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Holmes concludes that the gunshot was probably fired at a quarter to eleven, when Mrs. Allen heard what she thought was a door slamming. He notes that a shotgun fired at close range would be muffled but should still have been heard in the house.

l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: Sherlock Holmes says that the case hangs upon the missing dumb-bell. He jokes about the danger of an athlete exercising with only one dumb-bell, while indicating that the other investigators have not grasped its importance.

l: the wedding ring, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: The wedding ring was reportedly removed from Mr. Douglas’s finger and replaced beneath another ring, which Holmes considers an implausible part of the account. He also considers the possibility that an avenger took it because the vendetta might relate to Mr. Douglas’s first marriage.

l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: A bicycle was left concealed outside the Manor House and is treated as evidence of an outsider’s escape. Holmes finds it suspicious that a fugitive would leave behind the means of escape, while his colleagues travel to Tunbridge Wells to seek its likely owner.

l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VI
s: The investigation examines the statements of Barker and Mrs. Douglas, the timing of the gunshot and alarm, the blood mark on the windowsill, the wedding ring, the bicycle, and the missing dumb-bell. Holmes conducts experiments about how sounds travel through the house and plans further examination of the study.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Inspector MacDonald and White Mason identify the bicycle as belonging to an American calling himself Hargrave, who stayed at the Eagle Commercial in Tunbridge Wells and is described as a roughly fifty-year-old, fierce-looking man carrying a concealed sawed-off shotgun. MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave cycled to the house, hid his bicycle, shot Mr. Douglas, and escaped through the moat or by another route. Sherlock Holmes maintains that the murder occurred earlier than reported and that Mrs. Douglas and Barker helped conceal what happened and fabricated evidence of an escape through the window. Holmes later makes a solitary investigation focused on Mr. Douglas's single dumb-bell and returns asking Dr. Watson whether he fears sleeping with a lunatic.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Inspector MacDonald returns with White Mason, reporting that the bicycle has been identified and that a description of the suspected outsider has been obtained. He traces the suspect from Tunbridge Wells to the house and theorizes that the man shot Mr. Douglas and escaped.

l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: White Mason accompanies Inspector MacDonald in identifying the bicycle and investigating the suspect's movements. He questions why the suspect did not return to the hotel and expresses difficulty explaining how Mrs. Douglas could be connected with an American assassin.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes listens to MacDonald's theory but argues that the murder occurred half an hour earlier than reported and that Mrs. Douglas and Barker helped conceal the truth. He undertakes a solitary investigation centered on why Mr. Douglas developed his athletic frame with a single dumb-bell, then returns appearing to question his own sanity.

l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Dr. Watson sleeps in a double-bedded room with Sherlock Holmes and is partly awakened when Holmes returns from his excursion. He tells Holmes that he would not be afraid to sleep in the same room with a lunatic.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Mr. Douglas had seemed disturbed after visiting Tunbridge Wells, which Holmes and MacDonald treat as evidence that he had become conscious of danger. MacDonald theorizes that he was shot during his usual nightly round, while Holmes argues that the crime happened earlier than reported.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes suspects that Mrs. Douglas was involved in a conspiracy to conceal something and helped the murderer escape, or at least reached the room before he escaped. He believes she participated in fabricating evidence of an escape through the window.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes suspects that Barker was involved with Mrs. Douglas in concealing something. Holmes believes Barker helped the murderer escape, or reached the room before the escape, and helped fabricate evidence involving the window.

l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Hargrave is identified as an American who stayed at the Eagle Commercial in Tunbridge Wells under that name, carrying only a bicycle and a small valise. He is described as about five foot nine, around fifty years old, slightly grizzled, gray-moustached, curved-nosed, and fierce-looking, and he disappears after leaving the hotel.

l: Tunbridge Wells, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Tunbridge Wells is where Mr. Douglas had been the day before he appeared disturbed and where Hargrave stayed two days before the murder. MacDonald concludes that a man arriving by bicycle might have come from there.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave approached the house at twilight, entered the first room he saw, and hid behind a curtain. Holmes instead argues that Mrs. Douglas and Barker reached the room before the murderer escaped and fabricated evidence that he had fled through the window.

l: the bicycle, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: The bicycle is identified by the manager of the Eagle Commercial as belonging to Hargrave. MacDonald believes Hargrave left it concealed among the laurels near the house and abandoned it because it could identify him.

l: valise (Hargrave's valise), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Hargrave's small valise contained no papers or letters and had no identifying marks, but it was London made and held British contents. MacDonald believes the valise could have concealed the shotgun.

l: sawed-off shotgun (Hargrave's shotgun), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: The sawed-off shotgun was less than two feet long and could have been carried inside Hargrave's overcoat or concealed in his valise. MacDonald believes Hargrave brought it deliberately and used it to shoot Mr. Douglas.

l: single dumb-bell (Mr. Douglas's dumb-bell), The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes repeatedly returns to the question of why an athletic man would develop his frame using the unnatural instrument of a single dumb-bell. He makes a private investigation of this matter during the night.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: MacDonald attributes the murder of Mr. Douglas to Hargrave, who allegedly waited near the house and shot him with a concealed shotgun. Holmes disputes the reported timing, saying that the crime was committed half an hour earlier than reported.

l: investigation into Mr. Douglas's murder, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: The investigation advances when MacDonald and White Mason identify Hargrave's bicycle and obtain a description of him. Holmes remains dissatisfied with their explanation and pursues a separate line of inquiry involving the timing of the murder, the suspected concealment, and the single dumb-bell.

l: the open window escape, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: MacDonald theorizes that Hargrave escaped after shooting Mr. Douglas, possibly through the moat and then by another route toward London or a safe hiding place. Holmes argues that Mrs. Douglas and Barker may have helped him escape or reached the room before he did so.

l: conspiracy to conceal the crime, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes believes that Mrs. Douglas and Barker are in a conspiracy to conceal what happened. He says they aided the murderer's escape, or at least reached the room before his escape.

l: fabricated evidence of escape, The Valley of Fear, It was nightfall before Inspector MacDonald and White Mason came back
s: Sherlock Holmes believes that Mrs. Douglas and Barker fabricated evidence suggesting that the murderer escaped through the window. He considers this part of their effort to conceal the crime.

l: The Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Sherlock Holmes tells Inspector MacDonald and White Mason to abandon their search for the mysterious cyclist because they do not understand what they are investigating. Holmes discovers that the missing dumb-bell had been used to weight a bundle containing American boots, a knife, clothing, and a yellow overcoat, and he traps Cecil Barker into retrieving it from the moat. Mrs. Douglas then reveals that John Douglas is alive and has been hiding in the Manor House. Douglas gives Dr. Watson his written account, identified as the story of the Valley of Fear.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Sherlock Holmes advises Inspector MacDonald and White Mason to abandon their search for the mysterious cyclist while he verifies his own theory. He finds the missing dumb-bell and uses it to test the moat, then announces that the moat-draining plan has caused the person who hid the bundle to retrieve it. Holmes identifies Cecil Barker as the retriever and concludes that John Douglas is alive and should tell the complete story.

l: Dr. Watson, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Inspector MacDonald, and White Mason during the investigation and helps Holmes fish the bundle from the moat with his umbrella. Holmes refers to him as the historian of the group, and John Douglas gives him the written account of the Valley of Fear story.

l: Inspector MacDonald, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Inspector MacDonald reports that supposed sightings of the mysterious cyclist have led to arrests in East Ham, Leicester, and Liverpool. He initially objects to abandoning the case and to the moat-draining plan, but agrees to follow Holmes’s instructions and witnesses Cecil Barker retrieve the sodden bundle.

l: White Mason, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: White Mason participates in the discussion with Inspector MacDonald and agrees to follow Sherlock Holmes’s advice. He accompanies the others during the vigil outside Birlstone Manor and witnesses the recovery of the sodden bundle.

l: Cecil Barker, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Cecil Barker is found in the study retrieving a weighted bundle from the moat. He refuses to explain the secret and says it is not his to reveal, but Mrs. Douglas tells him he has done enough.

l: Mrs. Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Mrs. Douglas listens to the confrontation in the study and tells Cecil Barker that he has done enough. She then embraces the man revealed to be John Douglas and says that it is best for him to tell his story.

l: John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: John Douglas is revealed to be alive and hiding in the Manor House rather than dead as previously believed. He has spent two days preparing a written account and gives it to Dr. Watson as the story of the Valley of Fear.

l: Birlstone Manor House, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Birlstone Manor remains under observation while Sherlock Holmes and the others hide in a shrubbery opposite its main door and drawbridge. Holmes also studies an account of the ancient house and spends time alone in its study.

l: the Valley of Fear, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: The Valley of Fear is associated by Sherlock Holmes with the Vermissa Valley, a coal and iron valley in the United States. He suggests that the initials V.V. on the card by the body may refer to Vermissa Valley.

l: the murder of John Douglas, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: The supposed murder of John Douglas is the investigation that Inspector MacDonald and White Mason believe they are conducting. The revelation that John Douglas is alive shows that the apparent murder has not been fully explained.

l: the John Douglas case, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: Sherlock Holmes tells Inspector MacDonald and White Mason that their case is hopeless because they have not understood what they are investigating. He believes the truth can still be found through a shorter course than tracing the mysterious cyclist.

l: Hargrave, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: The mysterious cyclist is reported from numerous places, producing conflicting descriptions and several arrests. Sherlock Holmes says that tracing him will not help solve the investigation and urges the detectives to abandon that line of inquiry.

l: the missing dumb-bell, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: The missing dumb-bell leads Sherlock Holmes to suspect that something has been sunk in the nearby water. He finds it attached to the sodden bundle and later removes it from the bundle.

l: the sodden bundle, The Valley of Fear, Chapter VII
s: The sodden bundle is weighted with a dumb-bell and hidden beneath the writing table in the study after being retrieved from the moat. It contains American boots, a deadly knife, underclothes, socks, a gray tweed suit, and a short yellow overcoat.
